newsitem.title: USA: USDA's Glickman sees rebound in wheat prices.
newsitem.headline: USDA's Glickman sees rebound in wheat prices.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Wednesday he expected wheat prices to rebound from a recent plunge because supplies remain tight.

In a telephone news conference with U.S. reporters from Rome, Glickman said he was concerned by China's threat to temporarily block imports of U.S. farm products as part of a dispute over textile trade. However, he noted the threat had not affected commodity markets.
Glickman said, given the comparatively tight supplies, he expected "some upward pressure in the markets."

"I think that's already begun to happen...It did seem to fall extremely rapidly in a very short period of time. I'm concerned about that. I do believe those markets will come back. In terms of the EEP (U.S. export subsidy program), we have not made a judgement on whether to use it or not," he said.
China's threat of a temporary ban on certain imports "obviously concerns us," Glickman said. He said he had not seen a specific list of products that would be jeopardized.
Agriculture Undersecretary Gene Moos said the United States would press the European Union to promply assign a rice import quota. The quota was slated to be a topic at an EU meeting Thursday.
The quota was awarded as U.S. compensation for lost sales due to enlargement of the European Union.
"We still think there's time to get a lot of that quota filled between now and the end of the year," Moos said. "But the community has to act on that."
Otherwise, he said, the quota should be rolled over to next year.
Glickman said he would have "a rather informal dinner" on Thursday with EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler.
"We'll talk about all the matters, both in dispute as well as matters in common," he said.
Topics would include trade disputes, biotechnology, export subsidies -- "just a whole bunch of things."
Glickman refused to say what the United States would do if the EU refused to allow sale of genetically engineered foods.
"I don't want to get into the business of threatening anybody or talking about trade wars or anything like that," he said, noting there was not unanimity on the issue.
